questions.question: Constant-force interpolation assigns a fixed mortality force to each integer age interval $[x,x+1)$, where $x$ is an integer age. What does this assumption allow across neighbouring annual intervals?
options: The same fixed force must apply over every attained age.
The force must vary linearly within every annual interval.
Every annual death probability must equal its corresponding force.
Their constant forces may differ while each year remains internally constant.

questions.question: A table has zero probability $p_x$ of surviving from integer age $x$ to $x+1$. Can a finite constant mortality force $\mu$ over that year reproduce this endpoint under survival $\mathrm{e}^{-\mu t}$ for duration $t$?
options: Yes; set the force equal to one minus p_x.
Yes; set the force equal to zero.
No; a finite force gives strictly positive annual survival.
Yes; a finite negative force makes survival reach zero.

questions.question: Under constant-force interpolation, annual survival from integer age $x$ is $p_x=1$. What force $\mu_x^*=-\log p_x$ applies inside that year?
options: Zero per year.
One per year.
An unbounded positive rate.
A negative rate.

questions.question: Inside one age-year, a life has strictly positive constant force $\mu$ and survivor $S(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-\mu t}$ from the integer-age start. The density is $f(t)=-S'(t)$. Does constant force make this unconditional density constant?
options: Yes; the force and density are the same time-dependent quantity.
No; the density decreases as the original cohort shrinks.
Yes; annual deaths must be evenly spread over calendar time.
No; the density increases as fewer lives remain at risk.

questions.question: Annual survival from age 60 is $p_{60}=0.81$. Under constant-force interpolation inside that year, what is half-year survival probability $ {}_{1/2}p_{60}$?
A model cohort starts with $l_{60}=1000$ survivors and annual survival $p_{60}=0.25$. Under constant-force interpolation, at which age does its survivor count first reach $500$?
Annual death probability from integer age $x$ is $q_x=0.1$. Constant-force interpolation is required for that year. Which value calibrates its mortality force $\mu_x^*$?
options: $0.1$ per year.
$-\log(0.1)$ per year.
$-\log(0.9)$ per year.
$\log(0.9)$ per year.

questions.question: Annual survival from integer age $x$ is $p_x=0.81$, with constant force inside that year. A life has survived to age $x+0.25$. What is its conditional survival probability for another half-year, ending at $x+0.75$?

Annual survival factors at integer ages $x$ and $x+1$ are $p_x$ and $p_{x+1}$, both positive. Constant-force interpolation applies separately within each year. When does the proposed factor $p_x^{0.8}$ correctly give survival from age $x+0.6$ to $x+1.4$?
options: Whenever the total duration is shorter than one year.
Exactly when the two annual survival factors are equal.
Whenever the two endpoint ages have the same fractional part.
Exactly when the two annual death probabilities sum to one.

questions.question: An annual interval has positive endpoint counts $a>b>0$. Constant-force interpolation gives the midpoint count $\sqrt{ab}$. A proposed straight-line midpoint is $(a+b)/2$. How do the two midpoint counts compare?
options: The two midpoint counts agree whenever both endpoints are positive.
The constant-force midpoint is strictly larger.
Their order depends on the overall scale of the cohort.
The constant-force midpoint is strictly smaller.

questions.question: Annual survival factors are $p_{60}=0.81$ and $p_{61}=0.64$. Constant-force interpolation applies within each year. What is conditional survival from age $60.5$ to age $61.5$?

Annual survival from integer age $x$ is $p_x=0.81$ under constant-force interpolation. For a life alive at age $x$, what is the probability of surviving the first half-year and dying during the second half-year?

Let annual survival be $p=\mathrm{e}^{-a}$ with $a>0$. Model A has force $a$ throughout the year. Model B has force zero in the first half and $2a$ in the second half. Does agreement at the annual endpoint establish constant-force interpolation inside the year?
options: Yes; a positive annual survival factor uniquely determines every fractional value.
Yes; both models must have the same midpoint survival because their total forces agree.
No; the endpoint fixes the integrated force but not its within-year pattern.
No; Model B also changes the annual endpoint survival factor.

questions.question: Piecewise constant-force interpolation has distinct positive annual factors $p_x$ and $p_{x+1}$. Its survivor function is continuous at integer age $x+1$. What follows about the ordinary two-sided derivative of its log survivor there?
options: It exists because continuity of the survivor forces equal slopes.
It exists and equals the right-hand slope alone.
It fails because the survivor count jumps at every change of force.
It fails to exist because the left and right slopes differ.

questions.question: A proposed fractional table has counts $1000$ at age $x$, $900$ at $x+0.5$, $810$ at $x+1$, and $920$ at $x+0.25$, where $x$ is an integer age. Does it agree with constant-force interpolation throughout that year?
options: Yes; its midpoint is the geometric mean of its annual endpoints.
No; the quarter-year count should be $1000\sqrt{0.9}$, not $920$.
Yes; all the listed counts are positive and decrease with age.
No; its midpoint should be $905$, not $900$.

questions.question: In one age-year, $S(t)=0.81^t$ and $\mu=-\log(0.81)$. Set $f(t)=-S'(t)$ for $0<t<1$. After survival to $t=0.5$, let $g(0+)$ be the right-limit density of additional lifetime. What is $g(0+)/f(0.5)$?
